content: CD155, also referred to as the poliovirus receptor, is a protein encoded by the PVR gene in humans. It is classified as a Type I transmembrane glycoprotein and belongs to the immunoglobulin superfamily. The protein is commonly known as the Poliovirus Receptor (PVR) because of its role in facilitating poliovirus infection in primates. Under normal physiological conditions, CD155 plays a critical role in forming intercellular adherens junctions between epithelial cells. The precise role of CD155 in the immune system remains unclear. However, it is hypothesized to contribute to intestinal humoral immune responses. Emerging evidence also suggests that CD155 may participate in the positive selection of MHC-independent T cells within the thymus. The external domain of CD155 is responsible for mediating cell attachment to the extracellular matrix protein vitronectin, while its intracellular domain interacts with the dynein light chain Tctex-1/DYNLT1. Notably, the PVR gene encoding CD155 is specific to the primate lineage and serves as the cellular receptor for poliovirus during the initial step of viral replication. Structurally, CD155 is a transmembrane protein composed of three extracellular immunoglobulin-like domains, designated as D1, D2, and D3. Among these, the D1 domain is specifically recognized by the poliovirus. Low-resolution structural data of CD155 in complex with poliovirus have been obtained through electron microscopy. Additionally, high-resolution structures of the ectodomains D1 and D2 of CD155 have been elucidated using X-ray crystallography.
